item.title: Humanoid robot games put real-world skills to the test
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-23
BEIJING, Aug. 23 (Xinhua) -- Inside a makeshift restaurant, a humanoid robot gripped a snack with a pair of tongs, placed it in a microwave, turned the timer dial and then moved on to deal with another order -- all under the watchful eyes of judges. The restaurant-service contest, held earlier this week ahead of Saturday's official opening of the second World Humanoid Robot Games, offered a glimpse of a central focus of this year's event: testing robots not only in athletic competitions, but also in workplace tasks. Running through to Wednesday, the games have attracted 666 teams and 2,056 robots from 16 countries and regions across six continents, with team participation quadrupling from the inaugural edition last year. The event features 51 competition items, up from 26 last year, while the number of matches has surged from 487 to 1,301. Among the biggest additions are 21 scenario-based contests, covering settings such as factories, hotels, homes and logistics facilities. Tasks ranging from industrial assembly and housekeeping to emergency rescue and library book sorting are designed around jobs that can be repetitive, physically demanding, dirty, dangerous or difficult. At a service contest staged in a realistic hotel setting, more than 10 robot teams were given 30 minutes to tackle three tasks: moving luggage of different sizes, replenishing guest-room supplies and making beds. "Judges look at how many tasks the robot completes, whether there are collisions and how smoothly it performs," said an organizer of the contest. Even routine actions can pose demanding tests of robotic dexterity. In the restaurant contest, for example, robots had to turn a microwave timer to five minutes, with deviations of more than one minute costing points. They could also be penalized if too much liquid was spilled while delivering a prepared drink. This year's games have also introduced a dedicated dexterous-hand competition, featuring eight high-precision tasks including power-tool assembly, picking up beans with tweezers, weighing powder, prying open bottle caps and connecting flexible cables. The emphasis reflects an effort to bring competition tasks closer to actual workplace needs. Liu Weiliang, deputy head of the Beijing Municipal Bureau of Economy and Information Technology, said organizers had surveyed stakeholders in areas that include commercial services, landscaping inspection and emergency rescue, before designing the events. In one case, competitive tasks reflected worker duties at supermarkets, where employees may spend long hours at night restocking shelves, packing delivery orders and returning misplaced goods -- repetitive work that can be time-consuming and physically tiring. "Every task completed is effectively a trial run in a real-world scenario," said Liu. "There is no need to rebuild the same testing environment after the competition. Performance on the field itself provides evidence of commercial viability." The bar for autonomy has been raised as well. Except for the 100-meter and 400-meter hurdles, all track and other competitive events require full autonomy. In scenario-based events, fully autonomous operation carries a scoring coefficient of 1, compared with 0.5 for remote-controlled operation. Jiang Guangzhi, head of the Beijing Municipal Bureau of Economy and Information Technology, said that many competition rules are expected to evolve into practical technical standards, helping turn technological advances into industrial applications. "Once robots master these 'last-meter' skills, they can turn medals into orders and move directly from the competition arena to real-world workplaces," Jiang said. Xu Xiaolan, chairwoman of the Chinese Institute of Electronics, said at the recently held 2026 World Robot Conference in Beijing that China's humanoid robot industry had entered a critical stage of large-scale commercialization and deployment, with embodied intelligence products moving from small-batch trials toward broader adoption. Major technical challenges, however, remain. Wang Xingxing, founder of Unitree Robotics, said limited generalization capability is currently the biggest bottleneck facing the global humanoid robot industry. In controlled settings, he said, AI models trained on sufficient data can achieve task success rates close to 100 percent. But performance can fall sharply once the object being handled or the surrounding environment changes. Wang said "a ChatGPT moment in embodied intelligence" will come when a robot can be placed in an unfamiliar environment and complete about 80 percent of everyday tasks through simple voice or text instructions. He expects such a breakthrough could come as early as within two to three years, or within five to 10 years at the latest. For now, the games also serve as a testing ground to assess the technology's progress. Liang Hongjun, an official with Beijing Municipal Bureau of Economy and Information Technology, said the World Humanoid Robot Games were designed to give companies, investors and the public a more tangible view of the development of humanoid robots. "The industry is moving from telling technology stories to delivering real-world applications, and from pure technology development toward products and services," Liang said. That transition, he added, will require companies to focus on technological innovation, while governments and industry organizations work on opening up application scenarios, developing standards and defining safety boundaries. ■

item.title: Retired U.S. teacher begins China visit to renew friendship kindled in classroom, taming of desert
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-23
Ronald Sakolsky (C), Yin Yuzhen (R) and Yin's husband Bai Wanxiang pose for photos at an airport in Ordos, north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, Aug. 23, 2026. Retired U.S. teacher Ronald Sakolsky, who once supported China's desertification control efforts, arrived in Ordos on Sunday and was reunited with his friend Yin Yuzhen, a national model worker who has been planting trees in the Maowusu Sandy Land for four decades. Their story began in 1999, when Sakolsky taught English at a school in central China's Henan Province under a teachers' exchange program between the two countries. After watching a television news report featuring Yin's tireless work, he was deeply moved and raised 5,000 U.S. dollars to help Yin and her husband in their afforestation efforts against desertification. The saplings bought and planted with that donation have since grown into a forest of more than 50,000 towering trees. (Xinhua/Lian Zhen) BEIJING, Aug. 23 (Xinhua) -- Retired U.S. teacher Ronald Sakolsky, who once supported China's desertification control efforts, arrived in Beijing on Sunday for a visit aimed at renewing a friendship with the Chinese people that first took root more than two decades ago. The 69-year-old will spend part of his stay planting trees alongside his friend Yin Yuzhen, a national model worker who has been planting trees in the Maowusu Sandy Land for four decades. Their story began in 1999, when Sakolsky taught English at a school in central China's Henan Province under a teachers' exchange program between the two countries. After watching a television news report featuring Yin's tireless work, he was deeply moved and raised 5,000 U.S. dollars to help Yin and her husband in their afforestation efforts against desertification. At the time, the donation was a staggering amount that was enough for Yin to build a house, cover her children's upbringing costs, and even completely change the trajectory of her family's life. The saplings bought and planted with that donation have since grown into a forest of more than 50,000 towering trees. In May this year, Yin took to the internet in search of the American friend who had offered the donation decades ago, and their online reunion, a moment that moved many, soon followed. Upon arriving in Beijing, Sakolsky said he was eager to meet Yin in northern China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, reconnect with former colleagues and students, and see the forest with his own eyes. He also received mooncakes sent by Yin, a traditional Chinese symbol of reunion, and tomatoes grown in the desert. Invited by the China Education Association for International Exchange (CEAIE), his itinerary from Aug. 23 to Sept. 1 will also include China-U.S. teacher exchange events, a visit to Henan to meet with teachers and students at the school where he worked, a visit to the press briefing hall of the Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and visits to historical and cultural landmarks. The invitation is intended to further promote China-U.S. educational exchanges, convey the Chinese people's deep appreciation of friendship, and inspire more people to carry forward heartwarming stories of goodwill between the two peoples, a CEAIE official said. Over the decades, China has set up special funds, offered preferential tax policies, and mobilized farmers and locals in afforestation campaigns. Today, beyond dedicated local farmers like Yin, China's afforestation campaign also attracts large numbers of environment-conscious volunteers, especially young urban dwellers and international students. Official figures show that China has contributed about one-quarter of the world's increase in green vegetation and rehabilitated 152 million mu (about 10.13 million hectares) of sandified land between 2021 and 2025. ■ Yin Yuzhen waits for Ronald Sakolsky at an airport in Ordos, north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, Aug. 23, 2026. item.title: Chinese teenagers flock to tech frontline to touch the future amid AI study-tour boom
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-23
*To help children prepare for an AI-driven future, China unveiled an "AI Plus Education" initiative earlier this year, encouraging schools to take AI learning beyond the classroom through after-school programs and hands-on activities. *Moving beyond textbooks, students are flocking to tech giants, university labs and science centers, eager to get hands-on experience with cutting-edge AI technologies and see firsthand how the future is taking shape. *AI study camps are opening a new window onto how the technology is reshaping the world around them and how they can use it to make a difference. BEIJING, Aug. 23 (Xinhua) -- On a summer day, cheers erupted as clusters of children watched robots race across a soccer pitch, battling it out in playful matches, at a science center in Jiaxing, east China's Zhejiang Province. At a nearby workbench, nine-year-old Zhang Qihang was busy assembling a robot of his own. "Building robots is awesome! I can let my imagination run wild," he said, beaming with excitement. This was the scene at an artificial intelligence (AI) summer camp -- part of a new wave of study tours gaining traction across China. Moving beyond textbooks, students are flocking to tech giants, university labs and science centers, eager to get hands-on experience with cutting-edge AI technologies and see firsthand how the future is taking shape. AI STUDY-TOUR BOOM During this summer vacation, AI-themed study tours have begun to gain ground, with bookings surging 370 percent year on year, according to online travel platform Ctrip. To tap into the growing demand for AI-focused tech tourism, a travel agency based in Nanjing, east China's Jiangsu Province, began adding visits to technology companies to its trip programs last summer. "On our Shanghai-Hangzhou independent study tours, AI-related activities now account for more than 80 percent of the itinerary," founder Zhu Ping said. The boom is unfolding against the backdrop of China's broader AI boom, powered by a wave of homegrown models and applications. For a growing number of Chinese teenagers, AI tools such as DeepSeek, Kimi and Doubao are becoming familiar companions in their everyday lives. The number of AI enterprises in China had surpassed 6,000 last year, and the output value of the core AI industry was projected to exceed 1.2 trillion yuan (about 177 billion U.S. dollars) during the same period, representing a year-on-year increase of nearly 30 percent. Moreover, China was home to more than 140 humanoid robot developers in 2025, with shipments reaching 14,400 units -- accounting for 84.7 percent of the global market, according to an industry research report. To help children prepare for an AI-driven future, China unveiled an "AI Plus Education" initiative earlier this year, encouraging schools to take AI learning beyond the classroom through after-school programs and hands-on activities. The goal is to help students understand and use AI properly, while sparking curiosity, nurturing creativity and honing their critical-thinking and problem-solving skills. Today, the AI study-tour wave is sweeping through China's schools, as primary and secondary schools incorporate it into their educational programs. Parents are taking their children into the heart of the tech industry to see how AI transforms the real world. China's tech-tourism boom is also drawing international visitors keen to get a close-up look at the innovation behind "Made in China." Since opening in Shanghai in May, Unitree Robotics's first embodied intelligence experience store in Asia has attracted many foreign visitors. Victoria, from Denmark, visited the store last month. "I've seen some of the dancing videos, but it's really cool to see them in real life," she said, viewing the development of AI and robotics in China as "revolutionary, new and exciting." FROM AI USERS TO AI CREATORS Today's children are growing up as AI natives, already fluent in AI tools. But AI study camps are opening a new window onto how the technology is reshaping the world around them and how they can use it to make a difference. For Liang Yiduo, a Beijing middle school student, an AI summer camp run by internet giant NetEase offered a fresh perspective on the AI technology he thought he already knew. "I realized that large language models aren't just chatbots or simple tools," he said. "They can be assistants that work alongside you and help you create things tailored to your needs, like 'claws.'" "The goal of the study camp is to help children move from simply using AI to understanding it, creating with it and even building their own AI agents," said Wang Lijin, director and founder of Beijing Venus Future Education Consulting Center, which assists NetEase in running its study camps. Some study tour organizers design programs around students' interests and abilities, aiming to spark curiosity and encourage deeper thinking. Shanghai Qingbao Robot Co., Ltd., for example, offers students who enjoy building things the chance to assemble robotic arms and explore the mechanics of shoulder and neck structures. It also gives students a comparative look at the robotics and AI industries in China, the US, Europe and Japan, helping them gain a more balanced understanding of China's strengths and shortcomings. Wang Lei, the company's chairman, believes that study tours can greatly broaden students' horizons in science and innovation. "Through immersive study tours, students start thinking for themselves about how robotics can be applied to everyday life, from unmanned retail to automated pharmacies," he said. Some students are taking it a step further, learning to spot real-world problems and use AI to develop solutions. In the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen, a group of students spent six days in a camp turning ideas into an AI-powered product. "I've realized that learning AI isn't about showing off what I can do with it, but about using it to solve real problems for others," said one team member. "I want to keep learning AI so I can help more people in the future." ■

item.title: World Insights: Japan's two-front diplomatic push paves way for dangerous military expansion
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-23
TOKYO, Aug. 23 (Xinhua) -- From Monday to Friday, Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi visited Australia and India, where he talked up strengthening Japan's so-called "counterstrike capabilities" and promoted exports of Japanese defense equipment. Analysts said that Japan's ruling authorities are aggressively pursuing a "diplomacy of military expansion," stepping up efforts on two fronts: expanding arms exports and broadening the scope of military activities. In doing so, they are steadily chipping away at the constraints on Japan by the postwar international order and legal frameworks. ONE AGENDA, TWO TRACKS According to analysts, the topics on the agenda of Koizumi's latest visits showed that Japan is accelerating its "remilitarization" push abroad along two tracks: expanding arms exports and broadening the scope of military activities. On arms exports, the administration of Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has doubled down on efforts to market Japanese weapons and defense equipment overseas since it revised the "three principles on transfer of defense equipment and technology" and their implementation guidelines in April, lifting restrictions on exports of lethal weapons. Recently, it has been actively advancing the transfer of Japan's Abukuma-class destroyers to the Philippines. During his latest visits, Koizumi also sought to facilitate exports of the country's upgraded Mogami-class frigates to Australia, and the transfer of Unicorn communication antennas, which are installed on Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force destroyers, to India. Experts pointed out that the Takaichi administration's push to expand arms exports is not merely aimed at opening up markets for the domestic defense industry. It also seeks to forge closer ties with arms-buying countries on weapons systems, maintenance support, and parts supply, thereby further strengthening Japan's military influence overseas. On military activities, the Takaichi administration has accelerated efforts to expand the Self-Defense Forces' operational presence abroad, including sending a large contingent of combat personnel to the Philippines for joint military drills for the first time. During his trip to Australia, Koizumi reached a 10-year agreement with Australia, which will allow the Self-Defense Forces to use test sites in Australia to conduct test launches of long-range missiles to bolster so-called "counterstrike capabilities." Meanwhile, Japan and India also agreed to further deepen cooperation in joint exercises, with Japan Air Self-Defense Force fighter aircraft set to, for the first time, participate in a bilateral air force exercise in India scheduled for this year. Analysts said that the Japan-Australia agreement on long-range missile test-firing by the Self-Defense Forces on Australian soil signals a shift toward more sustained and institutionalized Japanese military activity in Australia. Japan's bilateral air force exercise with India, meanwhile, will mark another "dangerous first." Japan's push to deepen cooperation with relevant countries in maintenance, logistics, weapons development and other areas is, in effect, an attempt to extend its "strategic depth" and military capabilities beyond its borders, a move toward military expansion that runs counter to the principle of "exclusively defense-oriented policy." A "HIGHLY DANGEROUS" PATH OF MILITARY EXPANSION Since Takaichi took office, military and security issues have assumed an increasingly prominent place in Japan's diplomacy. While Koizumi was making his latest overseas visits, Takayuki Kobayashi, policy chief of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party, traveled to three Pacific island countries, primarily seeking so-called "security cooperation." In media interviews, Kobayashi also played up the alleged growing political and economic influence of a "particular country" in the Pacific island nations. Analysts said these remarks amounted to inciting bloc confrontation. Whether through expanding arms exports, broadening the scope of military activities, or reinforcing "bloc-based security," the Takaichi government's diplomatic moves are all paving the way for its military buildup and rearmament. These moves undermine the postwar international order and violate Japan's domestic legal framework, including its pacifist Constitution, posing a serious threat to regional peace and stability. Tessa Morris-Suzuki, professor emerita of Japanese history at the Australian National University, wrote in an article that Takaichi's desire to remove the peace clause from the Japanese Constitution is something to worry about. Japanese experts also pointed out that the Takaichi administration's exaggerated portrayal of the so-called "the most severe and complex security environment since the end of World War II" also represents a return to the dangerous militarist rhetoric. Veteran Japanese journalist and former NHK anchor Tomoyoshi Kimura said Japan once launched wars of aggression under pretexts such as "self-preservation" and "self-defense," packaging military expansion as safeguarding its "own security and national survival." Today, he added, the Japanese government is once again using the guise of "strengthening defense capabilities" to push military buildup, calling it "necessary for defense." But in essence, it is steadily marching down a "highly dangerous" path of military expansion. ■

item.title: Explainer: Why the latest round of Canada-U.S. trade talks collapsed?
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-23
OTTAWA, Aug. 23 (Xinhua) -- Canada will impose "dollar-for-dollar" tariffs on about 20 billion U.S. dollars' worth of American goods from Sept. 8 in retaliation for Washington's latest duties, Prime Minister Mark Carney said Saturday. The 50-percent U.S. tariffs, covering an equivalent value of Canadian goods, took effect just after midnight Saturday following the collapse of trade talks on Friday, further straining relations between the longtime allies. LAST-MINUTE BREAKDOWN Carney said he suspended the talks because Washington introduced last-minute changes that were "unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal," even though the two sides had appeared close to a mutually beneficial agreement earlier in the week. U.S. President Donald Trump signed three proclamations on July 20 to impose additional 50-percent tariffs on certain goods from Canada, citing Ottawa's "discriminatory treatment of American products." On Tuesday, Trump announced a three-day pause of the tariffs, which were scheduled to take effect on Wednesday, saying the two sides had reached a deal pending the finalization of formal documents. Carney said on Saturday that Canada had been prepared to remove its remaining retaliatory tariffs on U.S. steel, aluminum and automobiles if Washington substantially reduced its corresponding duties, and was also willing to encourage Canadian provinces to return U.S. alcoholic beverages to store shelves. "They asked too much and offered too little," he said. According to Carney, the U.S. proposals restricted Canada's ability to pursue trade arrangements with other countries, and undermined its protections for the French language, culture and national sovereignty. He did not disclose the details of those demands. Washington, however, blamed the breakdown largely on late demands from Canada, with U.S. tariff rates on heavy-duty trucks emerging as a key sticking point, Politico reported, citing people familiar with the talks. "They've always had the best deal, and they still would have an even better deal, but they didn't want that," U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told Fox News, adding that no further trade talks are scheduled with Canada. A UNITED RESPONSE In his televised address, Carney announced retaliatory tariffs targeting U.S. steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics, and promised to release the details in the coming days. "You're at war when you're attacked, and we got attacked," Carney said when asked whether Canada was in a trade war with the United States. Carney's tough position has drawn broad support across party and provincial lines. Pierre Poilievre, leader of the main opposition Conservative Party, called on Canadians to stay united against "unfair attacks." "Canada cannot accept one-sided tariffs that will deindustrialize our country. Nor can we accept a bad deal," he said. Several provincial premiers also backed Carney's decision. Ontario Premier Doug Ford said the prime minister had his "full support" for a strong response "tariff for tariff, dollar for dollar," urging provincial leaders to remain united as "Team Canada." British Columbia Premier David Eby noted that U.S. demands that Canada cut or reduce its trade with other countries would turn it into "the economic equivalent of the 51st state," which he described as "never acceptable" to Canadians. Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe said in a statement that while the U.S. tariffs will hurt, Carney made the right decision to reject an "unfair and unreliable" deal. A recent Leger poll found that 56 percent of Canadians wanted the government to take a hard line and make no further concessions in talks with the United States, and more than 70 percent supported stronger retaliatory trade measures. A BROADER SHIFT IN ECONOMIC TIES In his address, Carney argued that the decades-long expansion of economic integration between Canada and the United States was over. He accused Washington of using economic integration as a weapon. "We have recognized from the beginning that America has changed, and that we will not return to our old relationship," Carney said. He also criticized the shifting U.S. justifications for tariffs, ranging from fentanyl and a television advertisement quoting former U.S. President Ronald Reagan to bridge tolls and wildfire smoke, as lacking seriousness and severely damaging foundational trust. Since taking office in 2025, Carney's government has accelerated efforts to reduce Canada's economic dependence on the United States and diversify its trade relationships. Ottawa has sought to expand trade with markets in Europe and Asia, develop ports and energy corridors, remove internal trade barriers and double Canadian exports to non-U.S. markets over the next decade, Carney said in his address. The collapse of talks has also added uncertainty to the future of the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement. The pact remains in force, but the latest U.S. tariffs apply even to Canadian goods that comply with its rules, unlike many earlier U.S. duties. The scope for a rapid shift, however, remains limited. The United States still accounts for roughly three-quarters of Canada's merchandise exports, while cross-border supply chains in sectors such as automobiles and energy remain deeply integrated. Meanwhile, Carney underscored the importance of Canadian energy to the United States, noting that Canada supplies 99 percent of U.S. natural gas imports, 85 percent of its electricity imports and 60 percent of its crude oil imports. "I don't think they want us to stop sending it," he said.■

item.title: Chinese delegation for 48th WorldSkills Competition formed
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-23
BEIJING, Aug. 23 (Xinhua) -- China has formed its national delegation for the 48th WorldSkills Competition to be held in Shanghai in September, the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security announced Sunday. The Chinese delegation comprises 220 members, including 71 competitors who will participate in all 64 skill categories of the event. The contestants come from 21 provinces across the country, with 49 being students and 22 being working professionals. Their average age is 21, all within the age bracket from 18 to 25. Held every two years, the WorldSkills Competition is the world's largest international gathering of skills talent. It is scheduled to take place in Shanghai from September 22 to 27 this year, with nearly 70 countries and regions expected to send about 1,400 competitors. Since joining WorldSkills International in 2010, China has taken part in seven previous competitions, amassing a total of 93 gold medals, 41 silver medals, 28 bronze medals, and 71 medallions for excellence. The country has topped both the gold medal tally and the overall team standings for four consecutive editions. The competition covers a wide range of professional skills divided into six major categories, including manufacturing and engineering technology, information and communication technology, construction and building technology, transportation and logistics, creative arts and fashion as well as social and personal services. It will feature 64 skills, including seven new skills, such as software testing and unmanned aerial systems. The competition focuses primarily on practical work and generally does not include theoretical exams, with competitors instead completing hands-on tasks. A spokesperson for the Chinese delegation said the team will strictly abide by event regulations, compete fairly and with sportsmanship, and strive to demonstrate both skill excellence and a positive image, showcasing the craftsmanship and professionalism of China's young skilled workers. The delegation's official awards ceremony attire and competition uniforms have also been unveiled. Both outfits draw inspiration from the wooden structural craftsmanship widely found in ancient Chinese architecture, reflecting a heritage of artisanship and cultural confidence. ■

item.title: China's Chang'e-7 launch will not proceed in planned window this year
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-23
WENCHANG, Hainan, Aug. 23 (Xinhua) -- China's Chang'e-7 lunar probe does not meet launch conditions, and its launch therefore cannot take place during the planned window this year, the China Manned Space Agency said Sunday. The assessment was conducted following the principle of prudence, reliability and absolute mission success, the agency said. ■

item.title: Chinese robotics fair draws crowds as industry brews innovation
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-22
BEIJING, Aug. 22 (Xinhua) -- Unitree Robotics' blockbuster IPO, the bustling World Robot Conference (WRC), and the upcoming World Humanoid Robot Games, amount to a string of high-profile events which have combined to make this week a "super week" for Chinese robotics. Underpinning these events is a clear trend: China is swiftly becoming a global epicenter of robotics innovation, which is poised to reshape the way products are manufactured and the way people live. The numbers confirm China's significant rise in robotics. Data from the country's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology show that revenue of industrial enterprises above designated size in China's robotics sector had exceeded 300 billion yuan (about 44.24 billion U.S. dollars) in 2025, with an average annual growth rate of more than 20 percent over the past five years. Also, a report by California-based research firm Smart Analytics Global indicates that global humanoid robot shipments totaled approximately 19,100 units in the first half of 2026, with Chinese-made units accounting for over 97 percent of the total. More broadly, exports of industrial robots increased 13.2 percent in the January-July period, while shipments of surgical robots surged 3.3-fold year on year in the first half of 2026. Robots, AI products and innovative drugs are three new drivers of China's export growth, according to Science and Technology Minister Yin Hejun. This momentum has played out at this year's WRC, which is being held in a southeastern technology hub in Beijing. On weekday mornings, traffic ground to a halt for kilometers around the WRC exhibition hall, forcing the organizers to issue daily "travel advisories," a task that speaks volumes about the sector's red-hot vitality in China. Inside the venue, crowds are so dense they rival the throngs at CES in Las Vegas. WRC exhibitors this year have topped 300, up 69 percent from 2025, with the event featuring over 3,000 products, and roughly 300 making their debuts. Additionally, many are powered by large AI models, cloud computing and big data. China's vast and sophisticated manufacturing sector is providing a massive testing ground for embodied AI technologies, which are now being deployed on a large scale in factories and training facilities. According to an industry research report, by June this year, China had launched over 70 training grounds for robots, with another 46 either under construction or in the planning pipeline. "This week's IPO is just the start of the journey," said Aron Kisdi, managing director of Autodiscovery and Unitree Robotics' U.K. distributor, at the company's WRC booth. Unitree Robotics, based in Hangzhou in east China, went public on China's A-share market on Wednesday, the same day the WRC opened, and its shares skyrocketed 629.44 percent to open at 1,100 yuan. "It signals that the time in the lab is nearing an end, and we're pushing robots into the real world," Kisdi explained. On the exhibition floor at the WRC, many booths are displaying robots operating in real-world work scenarios. A logistics robot sorts parcels at a rate of more than 1,000 items per hour, while nearby, a pair of dexterous robotic hands smoothly folds a cardboard sheet into a packaging box. At UBTECH's display zone, robots perform automated loading and unloading of automotive sheet metal parts with zero human oversight, building on earlier trials at several car plants. Chinese robotics firms have, notably, already put robots into factories to test their capability of doing more sophisticated jobs beyond just basic handling. Elsewhere at the show, automakers like Xiaomi feature their own humanoid robots, underscoring how industry demand is fueling robotics innovation. The bustling expo floor in Beijing also features robots designed for emotional companionship, housework, convenience-store retail and coffee brewing, which can tap into China's massive consumer market, the world's second-largest in terms of commodity consumption for more than 10 consecutive years. "Robots are no longer only about flashy concepts and specs. They're increasingly focused on tackling real-life challenges," said Ren Jingwei, a manager at Zhiyuan Research Institute in Hangzhou. Also, this year's WRC fair is no longer just for curious onlookers. Industry players up and down the supply chain are busy exchanging business cards and phone numbers there in bids to forge new partnerships. One noteworthy shift this year is the considerable presence of dexterous-hand sensor makers, joint module suppliers and chip manufacturers at the WRC. These component suppliers, once supporters behind finished robots, have now also taken center stage in their own niche sectors -- a sign that China's robotics industry is maturing into a more sophisticated ecosystem. Humanoid robots could spur investment across precision transmission, smart sensors, AI chips and intelligent software, generating a huge market from R&D to after-sales service, said Xu Xiaolan from the Chinese Institute of Electronics. To many attendees, Beijing's robot show points to an upcoming transformative change in the industry. The "ChatGPT moment" for embodied AI will come in two to three years under an optimistic outlook, or within five to ten years at the latest, said Wang Xingxing, Unitree Robotics founder and CEO, when speaking at a WRC forum. ■
